newsitem.title: USA: RTRS-US VIEW - Australian dollar still seen strong post-Greenspan.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-US VIEW - Australian dollar still seen strong post-Greenspan.

text.p: The perception that the Australian dollar has developed an underlying strength gained further currency in the wake of the reaction to comments from Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan on Wednesday.
The Australian dollar held its own amid a flurry of activity in the U.S. markets following Greenspan's address to congress.
"It's been spectacularly uneventful," said Nigel Weston, the National Australia Bank's head of treasury sales in New York.
"I think it shows that in the near term it's (the Australian dollar) in that channel of 77.20 to 78 the figure."
A trader at large U.S.-based institution said that unless "unnecessary panic" hit during Australian trading hours, the Australian dollar was primed to begin its crawl back towards the 78 cent mark.
"And once it gets there, the barrier could be broken and we could see a half cent push," he said.
Australia's low inflationary environment and the Reserve Bank's apparent commitment not to change rates had international markets eyeing the Australian dollar, analysts said.
However John Simpson from Goldman Sachs suggested the dollar's fate continued to be guided to a significant degree by Japanese capital.
"The key factor that had been driving the Australian dollar had been Japanese capital input but that capital input hasn't re-emerged," he said.
Simpson said it was "technically extremely important" the Australian dollar traced back to 79 cents.
He added that Reserve Bank Governor Macfarlane's comments last week which doused thoughts of a near term easing in monetary policy had "sparked market participants".
"So far (Macfarlane) has done a very good job ... I think he is bit more articulate on these matters than his predecessor."
Zurich Kemper Investment Inc's global analyst David Hale agreed the Reserve Bank's comments had been well received internationally.
Despite continuing concerns about commodity prices, Hale believes Australia is on the cusp of a period of notable economic prosperity.
"I don't see too many clouds on the horizon," he said.
"I would say Australia may be entering the stage of Goldilocks," he said.
"Inflation is winding down, wages are improving, the retail sector could rebound," he said.

While the future looked promising, Hale tipped a significant downturn in the gold price as "Swiss officials have been telling people in private conversations" that they believed they would get legislative approval to sell huge supplies of gold.
